opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say the artists were central to it, not just a nice addition. When we started working on Glaze, we weren't coming at it as people who understood the art world. We were security and machine learning researchers. What changed everything was that artists came to us, told us what was happening to them, and then stayed involved the whole way through.

They shaped the problem definition itself. We could have built something that was technically clever but useless in practice. Artists told us what mattered: their style being mimicked, their livelihoods being undercut, and the feeling of having their life's work taken without consent. They also told us what wouldn't work for them. If a protection visibly ruined the artwork, nobody would use it, no matter how robust it was. That pushed us hard on the trade-off between how strong the perturbation is and how visible it is.

Then there was the user study. We had over a thousand artists take part, and many of them volunteered their time and their own work so we could evaluate whether the protection held up and whether the results were acceptable to the people who'd actually be using it. That kind of evaluation is rare in adversarial ML papers, and I think it's a big part of why the work had credibility both with reviewers and with the broader community.

So when people ask about the paper's success, I tend to push back on the idea that it was just our lab's achievement. It was really a collaboration. The artists brought the urgency, the domain knowledge and the real-world validation, and we brought the technical tools. Without them, I don't think it would have had nearly the same impact, and frankly, I'm not sure we would have built it at all.

r001.rationale: The response says more than a thousand artists took part in the user study and calls that evaluation a big part of the paper’s credibility and success.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd say the artists were central to it, not peripheral. When we started working on Glaze, we were security researchers. We understood adversarial perturbations, we understood how these diffusion models were being trained, but we didn't understand the problem from the inside. The artists did. They were the ones living with it, watching their names get typed into prompts and their styles reproduced in seconds.

So early on we did something that's a little unusual for a systems or security paper. We went and talked to them. We surveyed over a thousand artists, and we had a group of them involved from the very beginning, people like Karla Ortiz and others, who sat with us and told us what mattered and what didn't. And that shaped the research in ways I don't think we would have gotten to on our own.

One concrete example is the question of how much perturbation is acceptable. If you ask a machine learning researcher, they'll give you an L-infinity bound or some pixel-level metric. If you ask an artist, they'll tell you that the metric is irrelevant, what matters is whether the piece still looks like their work to them and to their audience. Those are very different standards. We ended up running user studies with artists to evaluate the visual impact, and that fed directly back into the design. The artists were effectively our evaluators for one of the two things the system had to get right.

The other thing they gave us was urgency and legitimacy. We weren't solving a hypothetical. We were building for people who were telling us in very direct terms that their livelihoods were at stake. That mattered when we presented the work, and frankly it mattered to the team's motivation. It's a different experience to publish a paper and then get thousands of emails from people who want to use it.

So I'd put it this way. The technical ideas were ours, but the problem definition, the evaluation criteria, and a lot of the reason anyone cared about the result came from the artists. I don't think Glaze would have been the same paper, or had the same impact, without them. And it changed how I think about doing research in this space, which is that if you're building protective technology for a community, that community has to be in the room.

r001.rationale: The response credits artists broadly with shaping the work and mentions surveying over a thousand artists, but it describes that survey separately from user studies and does not say an unusually large number of artists participated in the user study.

astra-6.text: I think the artists deserve a tremendous amount of credit. As researchers, we can bring technical tools to a problem, but we need the people experiencing that problem to help us understand what actually matters. Their perspective helps shape the questions we ask and whether what we build is useful. So I would view them as collaborators in the research, not simply as people who benefited from it.

r001.rationale: The response credits artists as research collaborators, but does not say that an unusually large number participated in the paper’s user study or attribute the paper’s success to that number.

sol-6.1.text: The artists were absolutely essential. They helped us understand what the actual problem was, what they were worried about, and what a useful solution would look like. As researchers, it’s easy to define a problem that’s technically interesting but doesn’t quite match what people need. Having artists involved gave us that grounding. So I view them as collaborators in the research, and a huge part of why the paper was successful.

r001.rationale: The response credits artists’ collaboration and input with the paper’s success, but does not mention an unusually large number of artists or their participation in a user study.
